UNIT.content: Acids and bases; Reactions of acids and bases; Salts.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
Communication and collaboration: as the learner sensitises the community on the acidity and basicity of substances used in day-to-day life such as bleaching agents, vinegar, salts, soda, juices, water, wood ash, antacids, lemons among others.
Self-efficacy: as the learner creates awareness on the importance of putting required amounts of salt on food to avoid cases of high blood pressure.
Digital literacy: as the learner uses digital devices to research on the applications of salts in day-to-day life.
UNIT.values:
Responsibility: as the learner carefully uses digital devices to research on the applications of salts in day-to-day life.
Respect: as the learner respects each other’s opinion while discussing with peers the meaning of acids, bases and salts.
UNIT.pcis:
Socio-economic and environmental education: as the learner discusses the effect of salts on the environment.
Safety and security: as the learner carries out experiments and presents findings on chemical properties of dilute acids and bases.
Learner support programme (peer education): as the learner discusses with peers the functions of acids and bases in biological and chemical processes (digestion, respiration, bleaching action).
UNIT.sep: Planning comparisons, observing, using simple models and arguing from evidence.
UNIT.careers: Laboratory support, agriculture, food processing and environmental monitoring.
UNIT.focus: Explain aqueous acidity, selected reactions and salt-air behaviour with distinct models and safe-use evidence.
UNIT.phenomenon: A fictional school store contains acidic vinegar, a mildly basic bicarbonate solution, a salt that becomes wet and washing-soda crystals that become powdery. Can one explanation account for all of them?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena: Microscale indicator/carbonate activities, teacher-controlled acid/base and acid/metal demonstrations, and labelled illustrative salt-exposure data.
UNIT.drivingQuestion: Which evidence helps us explain and use these substances responsibly? KICD: Why are salts important in day-to-day life? How do salts behave when exposed to air?
UNIT.storylineThread: pH classification -> biological/chemical roles -> neutralisation -> carbonate -> metal -> salt-water exchange -> fair comparison -> uses/risks -> communication -> assessment.
UNIT.subject: General Science
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
distinguish between acids and bases using the universal indicator and pH chart,
explain the role of acids and bases in biological and chemical processes,
identify products of chemical reactions of acids and bases,
classify salts according to their behaviour when exposed to air,
outline applications of salts in real-life situations,
promote proper use of salts in day-to-day life.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Time: 30 minutes within Lesson 10.Use G10.Work independently; give evidence for each explanation.No experiments are performed.All numerical data are illustrative.

sections.title: 1. Classify and explain an indicator result
sections.prompt: Classify P, Q andR in G10.State one limitation of using this result to decide whether a substance is safe.
sections.exemplar: P acidic, Q basic, R approximately neutral for these aqueous samples near room temperature. pH does not identify a substance or establish its safety; neutral substances can still be harmful.

sections.title: 2. A role and a limit
sections.prompt: Explain one role of acid in digestion and why “all bases bleach” is not a justified rule.
sections.exemplar: Stomach acid supports digestion, including providing acidic conditions for relevant digestive processes. Bleaching by hypochlorite involves oxidation of coloured substances; being a base does not by itself confer bleaching action. No medicine-use instruction is implied.

sections.title: 3. Identify reaction products
sections.prompt: For each named reaction in G10, give the products. Also state the products of hydrochloric acid reacting with sodium hydroxide. Explain why bubbles alone are insufficient to identify a gas.
sections.exemplar: HCl+magnesium→magnesium chloride+hydrogen. HCl+calcium carbonate→calcium chloride+water+carbon dioxide. HCl+sodium hydroxide→sodium chloride+water. Gas identity follows from the named reaction and supporting chemical knowledge; different gases can cause bubbles.

sections.title: 4. Explain salt-air behaviour
sections.prompt: Calculate both mass changes in G10.Classify each behaviour under the stated assumptions.Explain the relation between deliquescence and hygroscopy.
sections.exemplar: First change=5.80−5.00=+0.80 g; water uptake with solution formation is deliquescence.Second=4.50−5.00=−0.50 g; loss of water of crystallisation from the stated hydrate is efflorescence.Deliquescence is a hygroscopic behaviour with sufficient uptake to form solution; not every observed water uptake reaches that state.

sections.title: 5. Responsible application
sections.prompt: Describe one useful salt application, one related health or environmental concern, and one justified action.Include one safe rule about household cleaners.
sections.exemplar: Example: fertiliser salts provide crop nutrients; runoff can contribute to eutrophication; use appropriate quantities and prevent runoff into water.Accept another correct application with a linked concern/action.Never mix cleaners, especially bleach with acids.No personal medical prescription is required.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: Which evidence helps us explain and use these substances responsibly? KICD: Why are salts important in day-to-day life? How do salts behave when exposed to air?

lessons.title: Classify safe aqueous samples
lessons.observed: Indicator strips give chart-based pH estimates; class repeats or the illustrative G2 values are recorded separately.
lessons.learned: Universal-indicator colour and a chart estimate aqueous pH; for these samples pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 basic.
lessons.explained: For the named aqueous samples near room temperature, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic; pH does not establish identity or safety.

lessons.title: Acids and bases in familiar processes
lessons.observed: G3 supplies distinct evidence cards for digestion, dissolved carbon dioxide, antacid neutralisation and hypochlorite bleaching.
lessons.learned: An aqueous ion model helps explain acidity and neutralisation; bleaching also involves oxidation.
lessons.explained: Acidity helps explain digestion and neutralisation; bleaching also needs a substance-specific oxidation explanation, basicity alone does not imply bleaching action.

lessons.title: Observe neutralisation
lessons.observed: The class records pH rising as alkali is added, or labels the G4 fallback values as illustrative.
lessons.learned: For the named acid and hydroxide, neutralisation produces a salt and water.
lessons.explained: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide form sodium chloride and water; excess hydroxide makes the resulting solution basic.

lessons.title: Explain bubbling with a carbonate
lessons.observed: The approved vinegar/bicarbonate trial or supplied card shows bubbling.
lessons.learned: An acid with a carbonate or hydrogen carbonate can produce salt, water and carbon dioxide.
lessons.explained: The named acid and carbonate model predicts salt, water and carbon dioxide; bubbles alone do not identify the gas.

lessons.title: Explain an acid–metal reaction
lessons.observed: The teacher demonstration or observation card shows magnesium getting smaller while bubbles form.
lessons.learned: Magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid produces magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
lessons.explained: Magnesium and hydrochloric acid form magnesium chloride and hydrogen; this gas identity follows from the named reaction, not bubbling alone.

lessons.title: Classify water gain and loss
lessons.observed: G7 changes are+0.30 g,+1.20 g and−0.80 g; B forms a solution and hydrated C becomes powdery.
lessons.learned: Hygroscopic salts take up moisture; deliquescent salts take up enough to dissolve; efflorescent hydrated salts lose water of crystallisation.
lessons.explained: Under the water-only assumption A is hygroscopic, B deliquescent and C efflorescent; deliquescence is water uptake sufficient to form solution.

lessons.title: Plan a fair salt-exposure comparison
lessons.observed: Exposed and covered samples or the proposed comparison record time and air conditions; no change is a valid possible result.
lessons.learned: Humidity, temperature, exposure and controls affect evidence of water exchange.
lessons.explained: A fair comparison controls conditions; humidity and temperature affect water exchange, so a visible transformation within 40 minutes is not guaranteed.
